paragraphs.text: Dear sisters and elders, I hope you are enjoying a productive and positive day-to-day. I want to share with you some exciting news about who will be your mission leaders starting on June 30th, just 10 days from today. When I first realized that the Listons were not likely going to be able to arrive on time to take over from us due to the visa restrictions that most countries are imposing on their immigration process, including the Philippines—once I realized that, I started thinking to myself, well, who would be a great couple to be the interim mission leaders? And I immediately thought about President and Sister Solancho.

Now, of course, I have no say in this decision. The calling of a mission president, interim or not, is from the Lord through the First Presidency. But I hoped and prayed that it might be his will that the Solanchos would be called. They are great friends. But more importantly, they are great people. They have a deep kindness in them and are exceptional representatives of Christ and examples of his attributes. You will love serving with them. It will be different, though, and that is just exactly how it should be. President Solancho is different than me, and Sister Solancho is different than Sister Hughes. Different does not mean better or worse, it just means different.

You remember how we have often talked about maps. Your map is your personal view of the world. It is something you build over time through your observations and experiences. If you have an accurate map, it really changes how fast you can achieve your goals and how easy but successful your life can be. If your map does not reflect reality very well, if it is not very accurate, then you will spend a lot of your time and your energy trying to find your way to your goals. You will be lost a lot because that is what happens to people who don't have an accurate map of reality.

So how do you make your map more and more accurate? Well, there are two ways. First by experience. But experience takes a lot of time and can be very painful. It can even result in death. One wise person said: "Experience is a high-cost school, but a fool will not learn in any other kind of school." The other way you can build a great and very accurate map is by observation. You can study people who have accomplished goals like the ones you want to accomplish and achieve. And then you can find out from them how they see the world, what their worldview really is and how they came to acquire that way of viewing the world—or in other words, get that map.

I've encouraged you to learn from your companions and kabahis. Each of them have a different map, a different map from you. Their maps may not be, overall, any more accurate than yours is at this time in your life, but they will still have parts of their map that is more accurate than that part of your map. And you will have parts of your map that are more accurate than that part of their map. By learning from each other, you can learn truths about the world, thereby making your map better without having to have painful experiences. In other words, you can make your map better by observation.

Now who you observe and study is important because some people have really accurate maps and other people don't. So you could study some people and learn after a long study that their maps are really bad and totally inaccurate. You would have wasted your time and you would have learned things that were not true or accurate. How can you know who has a good map and who doesn't? Well, it's simple: "By their fruits ye shall know them." As we read in both the Book of Mormon and the Bible, a good tree will produce good fruit and good fruit can only come from a good tree.

As missionaries you have the blessing to learn from each other and from the teachings of the prophets and also from your church leaders and mission leaders. Your mission president and his wife are two of the most important people you can learn from during this season of your full-time mission. I can assure you, if the Lord, through the First Presidency, calls a mission president, you can be confident that man and his eternal companion have really accurate maps. That doesn't mean they are perfect, but it does mean they can really help you build your map into a much more accurate map that will allow for you to achieve bigger and more important goals faster and easier than a person with a bad map could.

So why do I remind you of this again? Well, simply put, the Solanchos have great maps. You have the privilege to study with them and learn from them. Whether they are here for only a few weeks or for the rest of your mission, it doesn't matter. You can learn some very important truths that will bless your life from them. But you must want that knowledge. It won't come if you don't proactively work at it. True study, real learning, is not passive. It is a very active process and requires your focus and energy. Passive people usually don't like the way their lives turn out. Proactive people usually do like the way their lives turn out.

But being proactive is not just a matter of being bold or aggressive. It is much more complicated than that. Being proactive requires situational awareness and self-awareness. It also requires deep personal responsibility. A person who has a sense and commitment to being personally responsible in all things learns more and faster than a person who is casual about their sense of being responsible for what happens in their lives.

Everything in life comes down to input, process, output. Your input is a function of your self and situational awareness. Being highly aware creates the optimal environment for observation. When you are aware, you can adjust and adapt and learn. You can exercise control or at least influence over your environment. When you are not aware, your environment controls you. The second step, process, is a function of responsibility. The more a person takes responsibility for their life and for what happens to them, the better their ability will be to process accurately and effectively the input they have gained by their awareness.

Since your output is what you get in life, it is very important that you increase your awareness, both situational and self. This increases the quantity and quality of your input. You must also begin immediately to take radical responsibility for who you are, for what you do and for what you have. As you increase your sense of personal responsibility, your process will become better and better, and these two improvements will radically improve your output, or in other words, your life.

Remember the four questions that will increase both your awareness and responsibility. First one: What do I really want? Second one: Why do I want it? Third one: What will I sacrifice to get it? And fourth one: When will I start? As you are honest with yourself about these questions and their answers, your awareness and sense of personal responsibility will grow, and your life will become better and better, because your map will become more and more accurate.

Well, elders and sisters, that's all I've got to say today, except for this: finish the day strong, be proactive, be self-aware, be situational aware, take responsibility for both acquiring input and for processing it really, really well. And remember this: we love you.
